Series::erfc¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::erfc() const -> Series
Series& Series::erfc_()

What It Does¶

Applies the complementary error function elementwise:

erfc(x) = 1 - erf(x)

That identity is the whole idea, but the reason erfc() exists as its own primitive rather than as a two-line composition is precision.

When x is large and positive, erf(x) is extremely close to 1. In floating point, 1 - erf(x) then subtracts two nearly equal numbers, and the small true answer is swamped by rounding error in erf(x). Past roughly x = 6 in float64, 1 - erf(x) collapses to exactly 0. The real value of erfc(6) is about 2.15e-17, which is a perfectly representable double; erfc() computes it directly and keeps it.

So the mental model is:

  • erfc(x) and 1 - erf(x) agree closely for moderate x

  • for x in the right tail, only erfc(x) stays accurate

  • for x in the left tail, erfc(x) approaches 2 and erf(x) is the one to trust

Properties that follow from the definition and from erf being odd:

  • erfc(0) = 1

  • erfc(-x) = 2 - erfc(x)

  • erfc(x) -> 0 as x -> +inf, and erfc(x) -> 2 as x -> -inf

  • erfc is strictly decreasing

The tail connection to the normal distribution is the usual reason to use it. The probability that a standard normal draw exceeds a threshold t is 0.5 * erfc(t / sqrt(2)), and that formula stays accurate for large t in a way that 1 - Phi(t) does not.

erfc() is an out-of-place unary transform: shape, dtype, and platform are preserved. erfc_() overwrites the current storage in place.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self, each element replaced by erfc(x). erfc_() returns a reference to the mutated current series.

The result dtype matches the input floating-point dtype.

Gradient¶

erfc() is differentiable. Since erfc(x) = 1 - erf(x) and the constant drops out, its derivative is exactly the negative of the erf derivative:

d/dx erfc(x) = -(2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-x^2)

The constant 2 / sqrt(pi) is 1.1283791670955126. The backward multiplier is therefore most negative at x = 0 and decays like a Gaussian in both directions. As with erf(), a saturated erfc() in either tail passes almost no sensitivity back to its input.

Examples¶

Example 1. The basic decreasing shape, crossing 1 at x = 0.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).erfc());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.9953, 1.8427, 1.0000, 0.1573, 0.0047]

The left tail rises toward 2, the right tail falls toward 0, and the midpoint is exactly 1.

Example 2. The defining identity holds elementwise: erf(x) + erfc(x) = 1.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.5, -0.3, 0.0, 0.7, 2.2});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.erf().add(x.erfc()));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000]

Example 3. Why erfc() is a primitive. In the right tail it keeps digits that 1 - erf(x) has already lost.

auto x = pluss::make_series({5.0, 6.0});

std::cout << "erfc(x)      = ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.erfc());
std::cout << "\n1 - erf(x)   = ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0}).sub(x.erf()));

Output¶

erfc(x)      = Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.5375e-12, 2.1520e-17]
1 - erf(x)   = Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.5374e-12, 0.0000e+00]

At x = 5 the two disagree in the last digits. At x = 6 the subtraction has collapsed to 0 while erfc() still reports 2.15e-17.

Example 4. Elementwise and shape-preserving on a matrix. The bottom-right entry is already in the deep tail.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {0.0, 1.0},
    {2.0, 3.0},
}).erfc();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 0.15729921],
  [0.004677735, 2.2090497e-05]]

Example 5. Non-finite inputs follow the limits. NaN propagates, +inf maps to 0, and -inf maps to 2.

double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({nan, inf, -inf}).erfc());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, 0.0000, 2.0000]

Example 6. The backward multiplier is the negative of the erf rule.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.erfc();
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.4151075, -1.1283792, -0.87878258, -0.4151075]

Compare with the same reverse pass through erf(): identical magnitudes, flipped sign.

Example 7. erfc() is floating-point only. Integer and boolean inputs raise rather than promote.

try {
  pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}).erfc());
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

erfc: dtype not implemented (float-only)

Example 8. erfc_() overwrites the current storage in place.

auto a = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
a.erfc_();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.8427, 1.0000, 0.1573]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • erfc() requires a floating-point input. Integer and boolean series raise erfc: dtype not implemented (float-only); call to() first.

  • Reach for erfc(x) instead of 1 - erf(x) whenever x can be large and positive. The naive subtraction loses precision and eventually returns 0.

  • Symmetrically, in the left tail erfc(x) approaches 2 and loses relative precision there; for large negative x compute with erf(x) or with erfc(-x).

  • The output range is (0, 2). Large-magnitude inputs saturate rather than fail.

  • Gradients vanish in both tails because the multiplier decays like exp(-x^2).

  • NaN propagates unchanged.

Summary¶

erfc() is 1 - erf(x) computed as a primitive so the right tail stays accurate:

  • strictly decreasing, bounded in (0, 2), equal to 1 at x = 0

  • the accurate choice for Gaussian tail probabilities

  • differentiable with backward multiplier -(2 / sqrt(pi)) * exp(-x^2)

  • floating-point only; convert integral inputs with to()

  • erfc_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::erf: the error function itself; erfc() is its complement and its backward rule is the sign flip of this one.

  • Series::exp: the primitive the backward rule is built from.

  • Series::log1p: another method that exists specifically to keep precision that the naive composition would lose.
